intro: Finding a cyst removal near you usually starts with a lump you can feel and want looked at properly, rather than a decision you can make on your own. You may be unsure whether it needs removing at all, or you may simply want a private appointment without a long wait. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who assesses the lump and quotes you directly for any procedure.
need_heading: What people searching for cyst removal near them usually need
need_lead: Most people want a clear assessment of a lump and a straightforward answer about whether removal is sensible.
needs: You have noticed a lump under the skin that is new, changing or growing, and you want it looked at rather than left to guesswork.
A cyst has become sore, inflamed or repeatedly troublesome and you want to discuss whether removal would help.
You have already been told it is likely a cyst but want a private appointment to talk through the procedure and what it involves.
You want the lump removed for practical reasons, such as catching on clothing or causing discomfort in a particular spot.
You would like the tissue examined after removal and want to ask about histology before going ahead.
context_heading: Understanding cyst removal as a private procedure
context: Cyst and lump removal is usually a minor procedure carried out under local anaesthetic, but only after an assessment to confirm what the lump is. Removal can leave a scar, so it is worth discussing where the cut would be and how it might heal. Any new or growing lump needs medical assessment first.

If you are considering a private clinic or hospital, hospital consultants should appear on the GMC's specialist register for their field, which you can check online. Private clinics providing regulated healthcare in England must register with the Care Quality Commission, and in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland different regulators apply. Many private specialists also work in the NHS, and if you have private medical insurance your insurer may require a GP referral and may limit you to certain consultants or hospitals, so check before you book.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe where the lump is and roughly how long you have noticed it.
Say whether it has changed in size, shape or colour, or become painful or inflamed.
Mention whether you have had a cyst removed before or whether this is a new problem.
Explain whether you have seen a GP or anyone else about it already, and what you were told.
Say whether you have private medical insurance and whether you expect to use it.
Tell us how far you are willing to travel for an appointment and procedure.
questions: How will you confirm what the lump is before deciding whether to remove it?
Will the removal be done under local anaesthetic, and what should I expect on the day?
Where would the scar be, and what can be done to keep it as neat as possible?
Will the tissue be sent for histology after removal, and how would I get the result?
What aftercare will I need, and who should I contact if the area becomes sore or inflamed?
What would happen if the lump turned out not to be a simple cyst?

faqs.q: Does a cyst always need removing?
faqs.a: No. Some cysts cause no trouble and can be left alone, while others become sore, inflamed or repeatedly troublesome. A proper assessment is the way to decide whether removal is worthwhile for you.

faqs.q: Will removing a cyst leave a scar?
faqs.a: Removal involves a cut, so a scar is likely, though its size and position depend on the lump and the technique used. Ask the professional where the scar would sit and how it is likely to heal.

faqs.q: Why might the tissue be sent for histology?
faqs.a: Examining the removed tissue under a microscope helps confirm exactly what the lump was. It is a routine step for many removals, and you can ask how and when you would receive the result.

faqs.q: How do I check a private clinic or consultant?
faqs.a: Hospital consultants should appear on the GMC's specialist register for their field, which you can check online. Private clinics providing regulated healthcare in England must register with the Care Quality Commission, with different regulators in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
